planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in spring in almost any soil, including poor, dry, alkaline, or compacted sites, in full sun; this extremely tough, fast-growing Asian elm tolerates drought and cold better than almost any other shade tree but has brittle, weak-wooded branching prone to storm damage and has naturalized aggressively across much of the dry western and midwestern United States.

directions: Siberian Elm is an extremely fast-growing, cold- and drought-tolerant tree introduced from northern Asia that thrives in poor, dry, or alkaline soils where few other trees persist, making it historically popular as a quick shelterbelt and shade tree on the Great Plains. The wood is weak and brittle compared to other elms, so branches break readily in ice storms and high wind, and the tree casts abundant winged seed that germinates freely, allowing it to naturalize and become weedy along roadsides, fence lines, and disturbed ground across much of the country. Because of this invasive tendency and its generally short landscape lifespan, many extension services now discourage new plantings in favor of resistant American elm cultivars or other shade tree alternatives. Where it is already established, little care is required beyond removing deadwood and watching for storm damage after wind events.
sources: USDA Forest Service — Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Plant nursery transplants or root hardwood cuttings in late winter to early spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; goat willow tolerates heavier, damper soils than many ornamental shrubs and establishes quickly from cuttings taken while dormant.

directions: Goat Willow is a European and western Asian native shrub or small tree grown chiefly for its large, plump, silvery male catkins that open in late winter before the leaves, among the showiest of any willow and a key early pollen source for emerging bees. Female plants produce smaller, less ornamental yellow-green catkins, so male selections are preferred for landscape and floristry use, and cut branches root readily in a vase of water. The broad, rounded gray-green leaves are coarser than those of weeping willows, giving the plant a sturdy, informal, somewhat shrubby outline well suited to wild gardens, hedgerows, and pond margins rather than refined borders. It tolerates damp, heavy soils better than most flowering shrubs and benefits from periodic renewal pruning to keep catkin production vigorous.

planting.note: Plant dormant hardwood cuttings directly into moist to wet soil in late winter or early spring in full sun; common osier roots so readily from cuttings that stock is almost never started from seed, and stems can even be pushed straight into damp ground along a streambank to establish a living barrier.

directions: Common Osier is a vigorous, upright willow long cultivated across Europe and Asia for its long, slender, flexible one-year shoots, which are the traditional material for basket and hurdle weaving and are still grown commercially for that purpose. Narrow gray-green leaves with silvery undersides clothe tall, straight stems that are typically cut back hard (coppiced) on a one- to three-year cycle to produce a continual supply of straight withies rather than being left to grow into a large shrub. It thrives in consistently moist to wet soil along streambanks, ditches, and pond edges and is also planted in dense rows as a living fence or windbreak, or for biomass and phytoremediation plantings, since it tolerates poor drainage that would stress most woody plants. Coppice stems every one to three years in late winter to keep growth vigorous and the withies straight and usable.

planting.note: Direct sow in early spring or fall onto well-drained soil; seeds need cool temperatures and light to germinate, so scatter on the surface and press in without burying.

directions: Atlas Poppy is a short-lived, drought-tolerant perennial from the Moroccan mountains that forms neat clumps of gray-green, lobed foliage topped from late spring through summer by a long succession of papery, tangerine-orange flowers held well above the leaves on wiry stems. It flowers far longer than most perennial poppies because new buds keep opening over many weeks rather than all at once, making it a reliable gap-filler in dry, sunny borders, rock gardens, and gravel plantings. It self-seeds modestly in well-drained soil, which helps replace individual plants as older clumps decline after a few seasons, and it resents heavy, wet, or poorly drained ground. Shear spent flowering stems to encourage further bloom and leave some seed heads to mature if naturalizing more plants is desired.

planting.note: Direct sow in early spring or fall onto well-drained, lean soil; seeds germinate best in cool conditions and should be scattered on the surface rather than buried deeply.

directions: Spanish Poppy is a short-lived, clump-forming perennial native to rocky hillsides in southern Spain, grown for its slender, branching stems carrying silky, burnt-orange flowers over a long season from late spring into summer, held above a low rosette of softly hairy, gray-green leaves. It performs best in lean, sharply drained soil and thin, gritty conditions reminiscent of its native cliffs and scree, and it tends to rot or become short-lived in rich, heavy, or regularly irrigated ground. Established plants self-sow readily where conditions suit them, continually producing new seedlings that keep a colony going even as individual rosettes fade after a couple of years. Leave some seed heads to ripen and shatter naturally if a self-sustaining patch is wanted, and avoid mulching thickly around the crown, which favors rot in wet winters.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container shrubs in spring or fall in nearly any well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Amur privet is among the most cold-hardy privets available and is a common hedging choice in the upper Midwest and northern Plains, where evergreen Southern privets cannot survive.

directions: Amur Privet is a dense, upright deciduous shrub from northeastern Asia valued above all for its exceptional cold tolerance, surviving harsh prairie and northern winters that kill the more commonly planted evergreen privet species outright. Small white flower clusters appear in early summer, followed by small black berries that attract birds, though the shrub is grown chiefly for its tidy, fine-textured foliage and its reliability as a formal clipped hedge or informal screen. It tolerates clipping into a dense, uniform hedge several times a season and recovers readily from hard renewal pruning if a planting becomes overgrown or gappy at the base. Because it can self-seed into naturalized areas in some regions, shear before flowering if seedling spread near wild land is a concern.
sources: USDA Forest Service — Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Plant divisions in moist to wet, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade in spring; Garden Loosestrife spreads by creeping rhizomes in damp conditions and has naturalized in wet ground in parts of the northeastern United States, so it is best sited where spread can be contained or is not a concern.

directions: Garden Loosestrife is a tall, sturdy European perennial of streambanks and marsh edges, bearing whorls of lance-shaped leaves along upright stems topped from midsummer by loose, branching spikes of five-petaled, golden-yellow flowers. It is taller and more vigorously spreading than its shorter relative Lysimachia punctata, making it better suited to wet meadow plantings, pond margins, and bog gardens than to a tidy mixed border, where its running rhizomes can quickly overtake neighboring perennials. Plants are unfussy about soil fertility as long as moisture is reliably abundant, and they tolerate standing water for short periods better than most garden perennials. It is unrelated to the far more aggressively invasive purple loosestrife (Lythrum salicaria) despite the shared common name, but gardeners in wetland-adjacent sites should still confirm it is not restricted in their state before planting.

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring or fall into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Sargent's Rowan is slow to establish and resents shallow chalky or waterlogged ground, so choose the planting site with care.

directions: Sargent's Rowan is a Chinese species prized by collectors for its unusually bold, large pinnate leaves and showy sticky red winter leaf buds, traits that set it apart from the finer-textured, smaller-leaved rowans more commonly grown. Large, flattened clusters of white flowers open in late spring, followed in autumn by abundant, long-lasting clusters of small scarlet berries that color at the same time the big leaves turn brilliant orange-red, giving an especially dramatic fall display. It grows slowly and eventually forms a broad, flat-topped small tree, so it suits a prominent spot where its architectural foliage and fruit can be appreciated up close rather than massed with other trees. Give it fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil and full sun, and avoid shallow chalky sites where rowans generally struggle.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or early fall into well-drained, average garden soil in full sun to light shade; this dense hybrid barberry takes clipping well and is widely used as a sheared or informal evergreen hedge and barrier planting.

directions: William Penn Barberry is a long-grown hybrid between Berberis verruculosa and Berberis gagnepainii, selected for glossy, spiny, holly-like evergreen leaves that take on a bronzed purple cast through winter cold before greening up again in spring. Small yellow flowers appear in spring but are of minor ornamental importance compared with the dense, mounded habit and tidy foliage, which hold up well to shearing and make it a durable choice for foundation plantings, low hedges, and barrier borders where the spiny stems also discourage foot traffic and deer browsing. It is markedly more cold-hardy than many evergreen barberries, tolerating winters that damage less hardy broadleaf evergreens, and it adapts to a wide range of well-drained soils without special amendment. Prune to shape immediately after the spring flush if a more formal outline is wanted, though plants also look well left to their naturally dense, rounded form.
sources: Morton Arboretum — Plant Clinic Shrub Guide

planting.note: Plant container-grown vines in spring against a warm, sheltered wall or trellis in well-drained soil in full sun; Red Jasmine is less cold-hardy than common white jasmine and benefits from a protected south-facing site in cooler parts of its range.

directions: Red Jasmine is an unusual deciduous, twining Chinese jasmine named for the Bees Limited nursery that first distributed it, notable among jasmines for its small, rose-pink to deep red flowers rather than the white or yellow blooms typical of the genus. Clusters of lightly scented flowers open along the previous year's wood in late spring, followed later by small black berries, and the plant forms an airy, loosely twining habit well suited to scrambling over a trellis, low wall, or shrub support rather than climbing to great heights. It is noticeably less vigorous and less cold-tolerant than common white jasmine, so it performs best trained against a warm, sheltered wall where reflected heat offers extra winter protection in marginal zones. Prune lightly after flowering only to remove dead or crossing stems, since heavy pruning sacrifices the following year's bloom.
